lesson.subtitle: Lesson 32 -- I Understand, However
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 32 -- I Understand, However
lesson.grammar_point: diplomatic disagreement (I understand..., however / I see your point, but / I am not sure I agree / with respect)

reading.rtitle: The Disagreement That Saved the Deal
paras: When two partners stop seeing eye to eye, the first instinct is to win the argument. That instinct is understandable, but it is usually expensive. Most business conflicts are not about facts. They are about a grievance -- the feeling that somebody was treated unfairly -- and no amount of facts will fix a feeling.

The best mediators start somewhere else. Before they talk about the problem, they acknowledge the person: "I understand why this is frustrating." It sounds small, but it changes the temperature of the room. Having said that, acknowledging is not agreeing. A good mediator can say "I understand" and, in the next sentence, "however, the date cannot move."

The second rule is to disagree with the idea, not the person. "You are wrong" closes the door. "I see your point, but the numbers do not work" leaves it open. When the disagreement is serious, "with respect" signals that what follows is firm -- and that it is still polite.

Finally, good mediators know when to stop. Some questions -- whose fault it was, who should have called first -- have no answer that both sides will accept. Instead of going back to these sore points, the parties agree to disagree on the past and look for a compromise on the future. In other words, the goal is not to be right. It is to leave the room with a way forward that both sides can live with.

listenings.text: I have mediated business disputes for twenty years, and almost every difficult conversation is decided in the first ten seconds. Most people start by defending their own position. They explain why they are right, and the other side stops listening immediately, because they are already preparing their answer. So I always start the same way. Before I say anything about the problem, I say, I understand why you are upset. That is not the same as I agree with you. I may not agree at all. But people can only hear a solution after they feel heard. Once they feel heard, I can say, however, and disagree as clearly as I need to. The tension goes down, and the conversation can move from who is right to what we do next.

Last year one of our shipments arrived three weeks late, and a client almost cancelled the whole contract. I was furious with the supplier, and on the first call I started by telling them they were wrong. That was a mistake. They defended themselves, I defended myself, and after an hour we had a list of everything that went wrong and no new date. On the second call, I tried something different. I said, I understand this was not easy for your team either. Then I said, however, we need a date we can trust. We never agreed on whose fault it was, and we decided to agree to disagree on that. But we agreed on a new date in ten minutes, and the client stayed.

extra_audio.text: First, you listen to each side alone and write down the grievance and the position. Then, you open the call by acknowledging both people before you talk about any solution. After that, you disagree with the ideas that do not work, politely, without taking sides. Next, you agree to disagree on the past, so that the call does not go back to old sore points. Finally, you end with a compromise that both sides can accept, and you put it in writing.
